property_summary: After calling go with a positive value, the contract C forwards that value to its owner so owner balance increases by exactly the sent amount (i.e., address(c).balance is zero and owner's balance increased).

For any caller and any sent value, after go() returns the contract's remaining balance is always forwarded to the deployer (owner); the mutant that forwards leftover funds to msg.sender can leave address(c).balance or owner balance different, so there exist inputs where this property is violated.

For any caller and any sent ETH amount when go() is invoked with a callee contract that accepts the forwarded call, the reference contract always ends with address(this).balance == 0 and the owner's balance increases by that leftover (i.e., the contract forwards its remaining balance to owner); the mutant that forwards leftover to msg.sender will cause the owner's balance to NOT increase for some inputs.

After any call to go passing through a callee that REVERTS the forwarded call, the reference contract always forwards any remaining balance to its owner (so owner's balance increases by the leftover and address(c).balance is zero), whereas the mutant sometimes forwards that leftover to msg.sender instead, leaving the owner not receiving those funds.

For every caller and sent ETH amount when the callee (target) consumes some or all forwarded ETH and returns (does not revert), the reference C always ensures its owner receives any remaining contract balance after go() returns; the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead will for some inputs cause the owner to not receive those leftover funds.

For any caller and any sent ETH amount when C.go is invoked with a target that REVERTS its call, the reference C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 because any remaining balance is transferred to owner; the mutant that sends remaining balance to msg.sender will leave address(c).balance == 0 still but the owner's balance will not necessarily increase—so the distinguishing universal rule: after calling go against a reverting target, the reference ensures the OWNER's balance increases by the contract's prior balance, which the mutant can violate.

For every nonzero wei sent to go by any caller, contract C forwards that wei to a predefined nonzero external target (which must accept the call) and then transfers any remaining balance to owner; the mutant replacing the target with address(0) causes the external call to behave differently (send to zero address succeeds but doesn't forward to the intended contract), breaking the invariant that address(this).balance is zero after go for some inputs.

For every caller and nonzero value sent to go, contract C always ends with address(this).balance == 0 (it forwards value to an external target which accepts funds and then owner.withdraws any residual), whereas the mutant sending to address(0) can leave funds stuck in C so address(this).balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to go(), if the callee target's fallback reverts then the call to target fails and C.reverts (so go() does not complete), but the buggy mutant calling address(0) will always succeed (not reverting) allowing go() to complete and thus the behaviors differ for some inputs (a failing external target causes the reference to revert while the mutant does not).

For every caller and any ETH value sent into go, the reference C will always end with address(this).balance == 0 (it forwards the ETH to the external target which accepts it, then transfers any residual to owner); the mutant that calls address(0) can leave ETH stuck so address(this).balance > 0 for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to go(), when the external target accepts the forwarded call, C always ends with address(this).balance == 0 (it forwards funds out and owner is paid); replacing the target with address(0) can cause some inputs to leave balance > 0, so the invariant balance==0 is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed amount/caller.
